1.0-5

What has been achieved

  • Each point is a link that entangles two matter nodes: how many pairs a second, how far
  • Colour and marker give the technology; the number beside a point is its year
  • Over metres, links make up to 7300 pairs a second; over 10 to 35 km, 2×10−4 to 2
Awschalom et al., PRX Quantum 2, 017002 (2021), arXiv:1912.06642; the links: sections 2.6 to 2.8
1.0-6
1.0-7
1.0-8

Every platform is judged on the same figures of merit

ηlink=γent/γdec
  • A share β of the atom's emission enters the mode; in a cavity C1 sets it
  • A fraction η of the photons is collected and detected
  • Links are made at γent, the success probability per attempt times f
  • A fidelity is quoted with its success probability
  • A stored link decays at the rate γdec
Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023), arXiv:2304.02088
1.0-9

What the two lectures teach

  • How much of a light beam one atom can take, and what sets the limit
  • How many atoms, a waveguide and a cavity each raise the coupling
  • How the coupling makes a memory, a source of single photons and a gate
  • How two distant nodes are entangled through photons, and at what rate
  • How ions, atoms, colour centres and circuits compare on one set of figures of merit

Both lectures and the problem set use one set of symbols

1.0-13
1.1

One atom and light

The driven two-level atom · Rabi oscillations · Γ and γ · saturation · the cross section · one atom in a focused beam

1.1

A laser couples the ground and excited levels of the atom

Hint=−ℏΩ2(e−iωLt|e⟩⟨g|+h.c.)
Ω=ΓI2Isat=𝐝eg·𝐄0ℏ
  • Ω is the full Rabi frequency: how fast the laser flops the atom
  • Measured: laser intensity I over Isat
  • Theory: dipole moment 𝐝eg, field amplitude 𝐄0
  • Δ=ωL−ω0 is the laser's detuning
  • |e⟩ decays by spontaneous emission at the rate Γ
Foot, Atomic Physics (Oxford University Press, 2005), ch. 7
1.1-1

The atom flops between the levels, less fully off resonance

Pe(t)=Ω2Ω′2sin2(Ω′t2)
Ω′=Ω2+Δ2
  • On resonance a pulse of area Ωt=π fills |e⟩
  • Off resonance it flops faster, at Ω′, and only up to Ω2/Ω′2
  • The curves leave out decay and hold for t≪1/Γ
Foot, Atomic Physics (Oxford University Press, 2005), ch. 7
1.1-2

Spontaneous emission sets the linewidth Γ

Γ=1τ=Aeg=ω03|deg|23πε0ℏc3
γ=Γ/2
  • The excited state decays at the rate Γ, measured as its lifetime τ
  • The natural linewidth, the full width of the atom's line, is Γ/2π
  • The dipole, and with it the optical coherence, decays at γ=Γ/2
  • Rubidium D₂ line: Γ/2π=6.07 MHz and τ=26.2 ns
Steck, Rubidium 87 D Line Data, rev. 2.3.4 (8 Aug 2025), Tables 3 and 7; Foot, Atomic Physics (Oxford University Press, 2005), ch. 7
1.1-3

Strong driving saturates the scattering rate at Γ/2

s=IIsat=2Ω2Γ2
R=Γ2s1+s+4Δ2/Γ2
  • Rubidium D₂, σ± cycling transition: Isat=1.67 mW/cm²
  • From here on s≪1 (single photon regime)
  • A classical drive is coherent when Ω≫γ
  • A single photon cannot be made stronger; instead to be coherent the atom must emit almost only into the photon's mode
Steck, Rubidium 87 D Line Data, rev. 2.3.4 (8 Aug 2025), Tables 3 and 7; Foot, Atomic Physics (Oxford University Press, 2005), ch. 7
1.1-4

One atom blocks an area 3λ²/2π of resonant light

σ0=ℏω0Γ2Isat=3λ22π
σ(Δ)=σ01+4Δ2/Γ2
  • σ0 is the rate R at s≪1 over the photon flux I/ℏω0
  • So Isat=πhcΓ/(3λ3): the dipole moment cancels, Γ and λ remain
  • σ0 holds for a closed dipole allowed transition driven with matched polarisation
  • Rubidium D₂, σ± cycling transition: σ0=2.91×10−9 cm², or 0.29 µm²
Steck, Rubidium 87 D Line Data, rev. 2.3.4 (8 Aug 2025), Tables 3 and 7, Eqs. 50, 52 and 61
1.1-5

An atom removes light from a beam by interference

  • β is the share of the atom's radiated power in the beam's mode, both directions together
  • The atom's wave has amplitude −β, so the transmitted power is T=(1−β)2≈1−2β
Lodahl, Mahmoodian and Stobbe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 347 (2015), arXiv:1312.1079, Eqs. 52 and 53; Steck, Rubidium 87 D Line Data, Eq. 58
1.1-6

A tighter focus raises β, but only over a shorter length

1−T≈σ0A≈2β,β≈σ02A
A=πW022,zR=πW02λ
  • The atom removes the power that falls on its cross section σ0
  • W0 is the waist radius of the Gaussian beam
  • The dark parts of the atom's radiated power enter the mode, β/2 each way
  • In an ordinary beam β is about 10−4
  • The focus lasts only over the Rayleigh range zR; a guided mode, below, keeps its area
β about 10⁻⁴: Windpassinger et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 100, 103601 (2008), arXiv:0801.4126, as quoted by Sheremet et al., Rev. Mod. Phys. 95, 015002 (2023), arXiv:2103.06824, Sec. II.A
1.1-7

How much light can a single atom absorb?

  • Tey et al. held one 87Rb atom at the focus of two aspheric lenses of NA 0.55
  • The probe beam is focused to a waist of about 0.86 µm
  • On resonance the atom removes 9.8 ± 0.2 % of the probe: this is 1−T
  • Since 1−T≈2β, this is β≈5 %
Tey et al., Nat. Phys. 4, 924 (2008), arXiv:0802.3005
1.1-8

Focusing harder does not allow β near 1 (strong coupling)

  • The formula 2β=σ0/A promises 25 % extinction at W0=0.86 µm
  • It is paraxial: the full calculation of Tey et al. gives 20 %
  • They measured 9.8 ± 0.2 %, β≈5 %; the lens and the atom's motion cost the rest
  • So the light must meet many atoms, or meet one atom many times
Tey et al., Nat. Phys. 4, 924 (2008), arXiv:0802.3005; σ₀: Steck, Rubidium 87 D Line Data, rev. 2.3.4 (8 Aug 2025), Tables 3 and 7
1.1-9
1.2

Many atoms in free space: optical depth and the memory

Beer's law and OD · the Λ system and EIT · slow light and storage · efficiency against OD · why a waveguide

1.2

A cloud of atoms attenuates light exponentially

I(z)=I0e−αz,α=nσ
OD=αL=nσ0L=−lnT
  • n is the atom density and σ the cross section
  • On resonance σ0=3λ2/2π (section 1.1)
  • T is the transmitted fraction of a weak resonant probe
  • Only the column density nL enters
  • The absorbed light is scattered in all directions: it is lost, not stored
1.2-1

A Λ system gives the atom a second long-lived state

  • To store a photon the atom needs a second long-lived state |f⟩
  • The probe, the light to be stored, drives |g⟩ to |e⟩ with Rabi frequency Ωp
  • The control, a strong laser, drives |f⟩ to |e⟩ with Ωc
  • Both are detuned from |e⟩ by the same Δ: two-photon resonance
  • |e⟩ decays at Γ; the coherence of |g⟩ and |f⟩ decays slowly, at γgf
Lukin, Rev. Mod. Phys. 75, 457 (2003)
1.2-2

In the dark state the two paths to |e⟩ cancel

  • In |D⟩∝Ωc|g⟩−Ωp|f⟩ the two paths to |e⟩ cancel: no light is scattered
  • The two fields are coherent: their relative phase sets that of |D⟩
Lukin, Rev. Mod. Phys. 75, 457 (2003)
1.2-3

The control makes the cloud transparent to the probe: EIT

Ωc2≫ΓγgfWEIT≈Ωc2ΓOD
Lvovsky, Sanders and Tittel, Nat. Photonics 3, 706 (2009), arXiv:1002.4659, Eq. 1; Lukin, Rev. Mod. Phys. 75, 457 (2003), Fig. 1
1.2-4

Across the window the index is steep, so light is slow

vg=cn+ωdn/dω≪c
  • The atoms that open the window also change the refractive index n
  • Across the window n rises steeply with frequency
  • A pulse travels at the group velocity vg, which a steep slope makes small
  • A weaker control or a thicker cloud makes the light slower
Lukin, Rev. Mod. Phys. 75, 457 (2003), Eqs. 2 and 3 and Fig. 1
1.2-5

Slowed light is a photon shared with a spin wave

  • The pulse moves at vg=LΩc2/(Γ·OD); the mixing angle is tanθ=2gN/Ωc
  • g couples one atom to one probe photon; N atoms sharing one excitation couple with gN
Fleischhauer and Lukin, Phys. Rev. Lett. 84, 5094 (2000), arXiv:quant-ph/0001094; Lukin, Rev. Mod. Phys. 75, 457 (2003), Eq. 15
1.2-6

A pulse is stored whole only if it fits in the medium

τd=Lvg=Γ·ODΩc2
τdWEIT≈OD
  • Inside, a pulse of length cτ shrinks to vgτ
  • It fits only if vgτ<L, that is τ<τd
  • Its spectrum must fit the window, 1/τ<WEIT
  • Both hold only if 1<τd/τ<OD
  • A large optical depth leaves room for both
Hsiao et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 183602 (2018), arXiv:1605.08519, after Eq. 1 and supplement Eq. S21; Lvovsky, Sanders and Tittel, Nat. Photonics 3, 706 (2009), arXiv:1002.4659, Eq. 1
1.2-7

Read-out is collective emission into the forward mode

Γfwd~NβΓ=OD2Γ
1−ηmem~ΓΓfwd~2OD
  • On read-out each atom radiates with the phase of the probe at its place
  • Forward, in the probe mode, the waves of all N atoms add up
  • Into every other direction each atom emits alone, at Γ
  • β=σ0/2A is one atom's share of the mode (section 1.1)
Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033805 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612083, Sec. III and Fig. 2
1.2-8

The memory error falls as one over the optical depth

1−ηmem≈5.8/OD
1−ηmem≈12/OD  or  38/OD
  • 5.8/OD is the error of storage alone or of retrieval alone
  • 12/OD is the error of storage followed by backward retrieval
  • 38/OD is the error of storage followed by forward retrieval
  • All are asymptotic fits of the optimum, the same for EIT, Raman and echo memories
  • ηmem, the energy retrieved over the energy sent in, is an efficiency, not a fidelity
Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033805 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612083, Fig. 4; Hsiao et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 183602 (2018), arXiv:1605.08519, Fig. 4(d); Vernaz-Gris et al., Nat. Commun. 9, 363 (2018), arXiv:1707.09372; Chanelière, Hétet and Sangouard, arXiv 1801.10023 (2018)
1.2-9

Hsiao 2018 stored and retrieved 92 % of the light at OD 816

  • Storage and retrieval efficiency 92.0(1.5) % at OD 816
  • Classical probe pulses of 200 ns with about 30 000 photons each, not single photons
  • The paper notes that it could be extended to the single photon regime
  • The storage time at 50 % efficiency is 1200 pulse durations, the time-bandwidth product
  • At OD 550 the efficiency decays with storage time, τ = 325 µs
Hsiao et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 183602 (2018), arXiv:1605.08519, Figs. 3 and 4(d)
1.2-10

The optical depth fixes the number of atoms in the beam

N=nAL=OD·Aσ0
  • A=πW02/2 is the beam area of section 1.1; the length L drops out
  • A waist of 100 µm at 780 nm gives A/σ0≈5×104
  • OD 800 then needs about 4×107 atoms in the beam
  • OD 58, a one-way error of 10 %, needs about 3×106
  • Hsiao's whole trap held about 5×109 atoms, a node of Yu 2020 about 108
Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033805 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612083; Hsiao et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 183602 (2018), arXiv:1605.08519, supplement; Yu et al., Nature 578, 240 (2020), arXiv:1903.11284
1.2-11

Free space cannot give a small area and a long length

ODN=σ0Amode
zR=πW02/λ
  • The same OD from fewer atoms needs a smaller mode area
  • A focused beam keeps its small area only within ±zR of the focus
  • So a tight focus is short, and few atoms fit in it
  • A guided mode keeps a small area over any length L
  • Along a waveguide OD≈2Nβ (section 1.3)
Solano et al., Adv. At. Mol. Opt. Phys. 66, 439 (2017), arXiv:1703.10533, Eqs. 5 and 6
1.2-12
1.3

Waveguide QED

Decay channels and β · one atom in a waveguide · β and C₁ · β across platforms · the memory on a waveguide · super- and subradiance · ordered arrays and chiral emission

1.3

Waveguide QED is done with cold atoms, solid-state emitters and qubits

  • (e) Cold atoms trapped beside a nanofibre, a glass fibre thinner than the wavelength
  • (f) Cold atoms beside an alligator waveguide, a nanobeam with a periodic pattern
  • (c, d) Quantum dots and silicon-vacancy centres built into a waveguide on a chip
  • (b, g) Superconducting qubits on a microwave line on a chip
  • (a) Platforms with weak coupling need more emitters
Figure: Sheremet et al., Rev. Mod. Phys. 95, 015002 (2023), arXiv:2103.06824, Fig. 2, with panels from Mirhosseini 2019, Foster 2019, Sipahigil 2016, Corzo 2019, Goban 2015 and Kannan 2020
1.3-1

A waveguide takes a fraction β of the emitter's decay

Γtot=Γ1D+Γ′
β=Γ1DΓ1D+Γ′
  • Γ1D is the decay rate into the guided mode, both directions together
  • Γ′ is the rate into every other channel
  • β is the probability that an emitted photon is guided
  • Γ′ is not Γ: calculated, 1.3Γ on a nanofibre and 0.8 to 1.1Γ on photonic crystals
Lodahl, Mahmoodian and Stobbe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 347 (2015), arXiv:1312.1079, Eq. 51; Asenjo-Garcia et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031024 (2017), arXiv:1703.03382; Bouscal et al., New J. Phys. 26, 023026 (2024), arXiv:2301.04675; Hood et al., Proc. Natl Acad. Sci. USA 113, 10507 (2016), arXiv:1603.02771
1.3-2

An atom beside a waveguide is a partial mirror

s=−Γ1D/2Γtot/2=−β
t=1+s=1−β,r=s=−β
  • Guided light can only go on or come back, so the atom's wave appears both ways
  • Forward it subtracts from the light, as in the focused beam: t=1−β
  • Backward it is a reflection: r=−β
  • The powers are T=(1−β)2 and R=β2; the rest, 2β(1−β), leaves the guide
  • At β=0.3, 49 % passes, 9 % returns and 42 % is lost
Lodahl, Mahmoodian and Stobbe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 347 (2015), arXiv:1312.1079, Eqs. 52 and 53 (T and R at zero dephasing)
1.3-3

Weak atoms add up to OD ≈ 2Nβ; one atom at β = 1 is a mirror

T=(1−β)2≈1−2β
TN=TN,OD=−lnTN≈2Nβ
  • For β≪1 each atom removes 2β of the guided power and reflects almost nothing
  • N such atoms in a row transmit TN: the optical depth is 2Nβ
  • As β grows the atom reflects more; the loss peaks at one half for β=1/2
  • At β=1 one atom reflects all the resonant light: R=1
Lodahl, Mahmoodian and Stobbe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 347 (2015), arXiv:1312.1079, Eqs. 52 and 53 at zero dephasing
1.3-4

A superconducting qubit on a microwave line reaches β above 0.999

  • A transmon is a superconducting circuit that acts as an atom at 5 to 10 GHz
  • Nearly all of its emission goes into the line: β>0.999, measured
  • Each qubit is made, placed and tuned on its own; about ten share one line
  • It works at about 10 mK, and its photons are microwaves
  • Over distance those photons must be converted to light: lecture 2
Figure: Sheremet et al., Rev. Mod. Phys. 95, 015002 (2023), arXiv:2103.06824, Fig. 2(b) and (g), from Mirhosseini 2019 and Kannan 2020; Table II
1.3-5

The cooperativity C₁ says the same as β, on another scale

C1=12β1−β=Γ1D2Γ′
β=2C11+2C1
  • C1, the single-atom cooperativity, is the guided rate over twice the rest
  • β is the guided rate over the total: the same information
  • Cavities are quoted in C1, waveguides in β
  • Half the emission is guided when C1=1/2
  • A cooperativity written β/(1−β) or g2/(κγ) is 2C1
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 4 (C₁ = g²/(2κγ), κ and γ half widths)
1.3-6

A nanofibre couples best at one radius, neither thick nor thin

Γ1D∝|𝐝·𝐄(𝐫)|2
  • Γ1D grows with the guided intensity at the atom (dot), 100 nm from a fibre of radius a
  • A thick fibre keeps the light in the glass; a thin one lets it spread far out: both couple weakly
  • Near a=170 nm the evanescent tail is strongest at the atom: Γ1D/Γ=0.30, calculated
  • A slow guided mode, as in a photonic crystal, raises Γ1D further
Calculated from the exact HE₁₁ mode (Le Kien et al., Phys. Rev. A 72, 063815 (2005)); Solano et al., Adv. At. Mol. Opt. Phys. 66, 439 (2017), arXiv:1703.10533; Lodahl, Mahmoodian and Stobbe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 347 (2015), arXiv:1312.1079, Eq. 49
1.3-7

On a nanofibre β falls steeply with distance from the glass

  • The blue curve is β (η in the paper) for a fibre 300 nm in diameter, calculated
  • β falls from about 20 % at the surface to under 1 % at 0.8 µm
  • The red curve is a tweezer's trapping potential; its minima are the trapping sites
  • β is 10 % at the first site, about 190 nm out, and 1.4 % at the second
  • An atom trapped a few hundred nm out has β of a few per cent at best
Figure: Nayak, Wang and Keloth, Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 213602 (2019), arXiv:1908.03319, Fig. 1(d), calculated after Le Kien et al., Phys. Rev. A 72, 032509 (2005)
1.3-8

β ranges from 10⁻⁴ in free space to above 0.999

PlatformβStatus
Free space, an ordinary beamabout 10−4measured
Cold atoms trapped at a nanofibre0.003 to 0.02measured
A few atoms at a nanofibre's surface0.13from a model

Sheremet et al., Rev. Mod. Phys. 95, 015002 (2023), arXiv:2103.06824, Table II; Lodahl, Mahmoodian and Stobbe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 347 (2015), arXiv:1312.1079, Table II; the other papers in the notes
1.3-9

Two colours of guided light trap atoms 230 nm from the fibre

  • Red-detuned guided light pulls the atom towards the glass (red curve)
  • Blue-detuned light pushes it away and reaches less far (blue curve)
  • Their sum (black) has its minimum about 230 nm from the surface, calculated
  • The red light is a standing wave: a row of trapping sites on each side of the fibre
Figure: Vetsch et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 104, 203603 (2010), arXiv:0912.1179, Fig. 1(a) and Fig. 2(a)
1.3-10

Nanofibre experiments hold up to 2000 atoms, each with β near 1 %

  • Each point is one experiment with atoms trapped along a nanofibre
  • The lines are OD=2Nβ: the experiments lie between β=0.3 % and 2 %
  • The optical depth, 7 to 40, comes from the number of atoms, not from a large β
  • A stored excitation came back as a guided photon in 25 ± 3 % of the trials
Vetsch et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 104, 203603 (2010), arXiv:0912.1179; Corzo et al., Nature 566, 359 (2019), arXiv:1909.08641; Han et al., arXiv 2509.22958 (2025), preprint; Pache et al., Phys. Rev. A 112, L011701 (2025), arXiv:2407.02278
1.3-11

On a waveguide the memory error falls as 1/(Nβ)

OD≈2Nβ,1−ηmem≈5.8OD≈2.9Nβ
  • 1−ηmem is the share of the light lost in storing it, or in retrieving it
  • Along a waveguide the optical depth is 2Nβ, so the loss falls as 1/(Nβ)
  • At the measured β of 0.3 to 2 % (grey), a loss of 1 % needs 15 000 to 100 000 atoms
  • At the lab's design value β=0.05 (point) it needs about 6000 atoms
Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033805 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612083; Asenjo-Garcia et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031024 (2017), arXiv:1703.03382
1.3-12

Two atoms in phase emit into the guide twice as fast

  • In phase the two waves add in the guide: decay at Γ′+2Γ1D, superradiant
  • Out of phase they cancel: decay at Γ′, subradiant; N in phase: Γ′+NΓ1D
Sheremet et al., Rev. Mod. Phys. 95, 015002 (2023), arXiv:2103.06824, Eqs. 15 to 17; rates of one atom at a nanofibre, calculated: Asenjo-Garcia et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031024 (2017), arXiv:1703.03382
1.3-13

A spin wave outside the light cone does not radiate

  • A spin wave is one excitation shared by the array, with phase kd per atom
  • For k<k0=ω0/c the wavelets add in one direction: a wave leaves (left map)
  • For k>k0, outside the light cone, they cancel (right map)
  • At k1D, outside the cone, the spin wave emits only into the guide
  • One spin wave can be subradiant into free space and superradiant into the guide
Asenjo-Garcia et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031024 (2017), arXiv:1703.03382; the band diagram is schematic, the maps calculated for scalar waves
1.3-14

Selective radiance sends one collective mode into the guide

  • (a) The guided rate Γ1D (blue) peaks at ±k1D
  • Only inside the light cone (grey) do the modes radiate into free space, at Γ′ (green)
  • (b) The best ratio Γ1D/Γ′ grows as 0.0053N2, calculated
  • Independent atoms would give a ratio that grows only as N
  • Such a mode is subradiant into free space and superradiant into the guide
Figure: Asenjo-Garcia et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031024 (2017), arXiv:1703.03382, Fig. 15, CC BY
1.3-15

Collective storage in an array can beat 1/N, in theory

  • Independent atoms lose 5.8/OD≈10/N (blue)
  • A Gaussian spin wave still loses 4.1/N: it scatters at the end of the chain
  • A spin wave concentrated near the exit loses about 26/N2
  • With a control rising towards the exit the loss falls as 0.15e−N/23
  • Calculated for an array on a nanofibre; no such experiment exists yet
Asenjo-Garcia et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031024 (2017), arXiv:1703.03382, Eqs. 26 and 29, Figs. 14(c), 16(d) and 18(d); Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033805 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612083
1.3-16

Guided light can be chiral and couple atoms at any range

  • Near the glass the guided field rotates, opposite ways for the two directions (black)
  • A σ+ dipole (blue) turns one way, so it emits mostly forward: chiral coupling
  • In a waveguide designed for atoms (a), 92 % of the guided light goes one way, calculated
  • The guided mode does not spread, so atoms far apart along the fibre emit together
  • Seen on nanofibres: decay at 1.10±0.02Γ from a few atoms, a superradiant burst from 1000
Left: calculated from the exact HE₁₁ mode for the nanofibre of Lodahl et al., Nature 541, 473 (2017), arXiv:1608.00446, Fig. 2. Figure (a): Bouscal et al., New J. Phys. 26, 023026 (2024), arXiv:2301.04675, Fig. 4(a); Solano et al., Nat. Commun. 8, 1857 (2017), arXiv:1704.07486; Liedl et al., Phys. Rev. X 14, 011020 (2024), arXiv:2211.08940
1.3-17
1.4

Cavity QED and the cavity gate

Two mirrors · the three rates g, κ and γ · the cooperativity C₁ · one atom in a cavity · a photon in and out · the reflection gate · memory in a cavity

1.4

Two mirrors store light at a comb of resonant frequencies

FSR=c2L,F=FSRFWHM
  • Light passes when a whole number of half wavelengths fits between the mirrors
  • The lines are spaced by the free spectral range, FSR, for mirrors a length L apart
  • The finesse F is the measured spacing of the lines over their full width, FWHM
  • Better mirrors give narrower lines
  • F≈π/(1−R) for two mirrors of power reflectivity R near 1
1.4-1

A photon crosses the cavity about 2F/π times

  • One pass removes OD1=σ0/(πw02/2), the atom's cross-section over the beam's area
  • The photon makes about 2F/π passes before it leaks out, each adding OD1
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 1; Webb et al., Nano Convergence 13, 35 (2026), p. 4 and Eq. 7
1.4-2

The curvature of the mirrors sets the waist of the mode

w02=λ2πL(2ρ−L)(ρ1=ρ2=ρ)
  • The waist w0 is the radius of the mode at its narrowest point, between the mirrors
  • Radii of curvature ρ1 and ρ2 give a stable mode for 0≤(1−L/ρ1)(1−L/ρ2)≤1
  • The mode between the mirrors has the volume V=πw02L/4
  • Strongly curved mirrors close together give a small waist
  • w0=1.3 µm for ρ=50 µm and L=2 µm at 780 nm, calculated
Saleh and Teich, Fundamentals of Photonics (Wiley, 1991), Eqs. 9.2-14 and 9.2-16; Hunger et al., New J. Phys. 12, 065038 (2010), arXiv:1005.0067, Eq. 6
1.4-3

Three measured rates describe one atom in a cavity

  • 2g is the vacuum Rabi splitting: one atom splits the cavity's line in two, 2g apart
  • In time, atom and mode exchange one quantum at 2g, the vacuum Rabi frequency
  • κ is half the width of the empty cavity's line: its field leaks out at πc/(2LF)
  • γ=Γ/2 is half the atom's natural linewidth: its decay out of the side
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 2
1.4-4

g is the Rabi frequency in the field of a single photon

g=λπw03cΓ2L=dE1ℏ
  • A laser drives the Rabi frequency Ω=Γs/2, with s=I/Isat
  • One photon stored in the mode drives g
  • Measured: λ, linewidth Γ, waist w0, length L
  • Theory: dipole moment d, one photon's field E1=ℏω/2ε0V
  • Rb, L=0.5 mm, w0=30 µm: g/2π=7.7MHz, calculated
  • The experiment reports up to 5 MHz
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 2; Ritter et al., Nature 484, 195 (2012), arXiv:1202.5955
1.4-5

The cooperativity C₁ compares the coupling with the losses

C1=g22κγ=3Fλ2π3w02
  • C1 of order 1 or more means the coupling g beats the two losses, κ and γ
  • It is the count of the film: about 2F/π passes, each absorbing OD1, make 2C1
  • The length cancels: only the finesse F and the waist w0 remain
  • Other forms in papers are converted in the table of the introduction
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 4; Hunger et al., New J. Phys. 12, 065038 (2010), arXiv:1005.0067, Eq. 22
1.4-6

Mirrors on fibre tips make a cavity with a micrometre waist

QuantityValue
Finesse F37 000 ± 5000 measured; 130 000 or more projected
Smallest mode, calculatedw0=1.3 µm and V≈5.5λ3 for ρ=50 µm, L≈2 µm
Share of the fibre's light entering the cavity mode0.72 or more measured, about 0.85 realistic, 0.979 in theory
Cooperativity C1 for Rb, calculatedabout 1300 at the measured F, 4560 at the projected F (w0=1.3 µm)
Hunger et al., New J. Phys. 12, 065038 (2010), arXiv:1005.0067
1.4-7

One atom with C₁ ≥ 1 blocks the light through a cavity

TatomTempty=1(1+2C1)2
  • One atom lowers the transmission T of a probe on resonance
  • At C1=1 one atom cuts T to 1/9, at C1=10 to 0.002
  • The drop is a direct measurement of C1
  • Papers quote Nc=1/C1, the critical atom number: below 1, one atom is enough
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 16b; further reading: Tanji-Suzuki et al., Adv. At. Mol. Opt. Phys. 60, 201 (2011), arXiv:1104.3594
1.4-8

N atoms in the mode act together, with CN=NC1

CN=NC1
  • N atoms share one excitation, and their couplings add: g becomes gN
  • For atoms at the antinodes of the standing wave the cooperativity is N times larger
  • Atoms spread along the axis see half the intensity on average: CN=NC1/2
  • An ensemble raises CN, never C1; the gate of this section needs C1
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, p. 4; Tanji-Suzuki et al., Adv. At. Mol. Opt. Phys. 60, 201 (2011), arXiv:1104.3594, section 1.4
1.4-9

Atom and cavity pass one quantum back and forth at 2g

Pe(t)=cos2(gt)
  • Pe is the probability that the atom, excited at t=0, is still excited
  • The atom emits a photon into the mode and takes it back: the vacuum Rabi oscillation
  • Dashed, without loss; solid, with (g,κ,γ)/2π=(7,2.5,3) MHz
  • With loss the photon leaks out or the atom decays within a cycle or two
  • The oscillation shows only when g exceeds κ and γ
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 2 and Fig. 3a; Haroche and Raimond, Exploring the Quantum (Oxford, 2006)
1.4-10

The coupled atom and mode have pairs of levels split by 2g√n

H/ℏ=ωaσ+σ−+ωca†a+g(aσ++a†σ−)
  • The three terms: the atom's energy, the energy of the photons, and the exchange of one quantum at the rate g
  • Without coupling, |g,n⟩ (atom in the ground state, n photons) and |e,n−1⟩ have the same energy
  • The coupling splits each pair by 2gn
  • The lowest pair, split by 2g, is the oscillation of the last slide seen in energy
  • This is the Jaynes-Cummings model: one two-level atom and one mode, without loss
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 2; Haroche and Raimond, Exploring the Quantum (Oxford, 2006)
1.4-11

The largest of g, κ and γ decides how atom and cavity behave

RegimeConditionWhat happens
Strong couplingg>κ,γAtom and mode exchange the photon back and forth; the line splits by 2g
Purcell (bad cavity)κ>g>γ, C1≳1No exchange: the atom emits into the mode, faster than in free space
Weak couplingC1≪1The atom emits mostly into free space, as without a cavity
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Fig. 6 and Eqs. 12 and 16
1.4-12

Strong coupling: for g above κ and γ the line splits in two

  • Strong coupling, g≫κ,γ: the photon is exchanged before either loses it
  • A weak probe finds two lines at ±g in place of one: the vacuum Rabi splitting, 2g
  • The splitting is how g is measured
  • Drawn for (g,κ,γ)/2π=(7,2.5,3) MHz, where C1=3.3
  • Each line is about κ+γ wide
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Fig. 6 and Eq. 16
1.4-13

Purcell regime: a leaky cavity makes the atom emit faster

γc=g2κ=2C1γ
  • Purcell regime, κ≫g≫γ: the photon leaves before the atom takes it back
  • No oscillation and no splitting: the atom decays once, faster than in free space
  • It emits into the mode at γc and to the side at γ; its line broadens to γ(1+2C1)
  • A shorter lifetime measures C1: 26 ns to 3.0 ns means 2C1=7.7
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 12; Tiecke et al., Nature 508, 241 (2014), arXiv:1404.5615
1.4-14

A cavity can speed up the atom's decay, or slow it down

  • Spontaneous emission is not fixed by the atom: its rate follows the modes around it
  • On resonance with the cavity the atom decays 1+2C1 times faster (Purcell)
  • Tuned away, with mirrors around it, it decays slower: inhibited emission
  • Rydberg atoms between plates under λ/2 apart lived at least 20 times longer
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 12; Purcell, Phys. Rev. 69, 681 (1946); Kleppner, Phys. Rev. Lett. 47, 233 (1981); Hulet, Hilfer and Kleppner, Phys. Rev. Lett. 55, 2137 (1985)
1.4-15

A cavity and a waveguide are judged by the same number, β

β=γcγc+γ=2C11+2C1
  • β is the share of the emission into the wanted mode: cavity mode or guided mode
  • So C1=β/(2(1−β)) is one scale for both
  • For large C1 the lost share is 1−β≈1/(2C1)
  • A nanofibre cavity, between two fibre mirrors, is both: C1=2.7 for one Cs atom
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889; Sheremet et al., Rev. Mod. Phys. 95, 015002 (2023), arXiv:2103.06824; Pache et al., Phys. Rev. A 112, L011701 (2025), arXiv:2407.02278; Nayak, Wang and Keloth, Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 213602 (2019), arXiv:1908.03319
1.4-16

How do we retrieve a stored photon on demand?

  • The aim: one photon, in the cavity's mode, at a time we choose
  • The atom has two ground states, |g⟩ and |f⟩, and an excited state |e⟩
  • A control laser, Ω, lifts it from |g⟩; the cavity, g, brings it down to |f⟩
  • On the way the cavity gains one photon, which leaves through the mirror
  • In |f⟩ the laser no longer acts: one pulse gives one photon
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, section I.E; emission and absorption, sections III.A and IV.A.1
1.4-17

Raising the control laser turns the atom's state into a photon

|D⟩=cosθ|g,0⟩−sinθ|f,1⟩
  • A dark state, as in EIT: no part in |e⟩, so no spontaneous emission
  • With tanθ=Ω/2g it is |g,0⟩ for Ω≪2g and |f,1⟩ for Ω≫2g
  • Raising Ω slowly is vacuum STIRAP, stimulated Raman adiabatic passage
  • The photon leaks out with a shape set by Ω(t); run backwards, the atom absorbs one
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, section I.E, Eq. 19; sections III.A and IV.A.1; Ritter et al., Nature 484, 195 (2012), arXiv:1202.5955
1.4-18

Two atoms in two cavities passed a qubit through a fibre

  • A qubit passed from atom to atom with fidelity 84(1) % at 0.2 % success
  • A lower bound, post-selected: a success shows only when the read-out photon is detected
Ritter et al., Nature 484, 195 (2012), arXiv:1202.5955
1.4-19

A Rydberg atom detects a photon without absorbing it

  • A microwave cavity holds 0 or 1 photon; Rydberg atoms cross it one at a time
  • An atom in level g absorbs the photon and gives it back, one full Rabi cycle: the state changes sign
  • Two π/2 pulses, R1 before and R2 after the cavity, turn that sign into the final level, g or i
  • The photon is still in the cavity: a second atom detects it again
  • One photon gives a phase of π; the gate of the next slides reads the same phase on the light
Figure: Nogues et al., Nature 400, 239 (1999), Fig. 1 (left); Gleyzes et al., Nature 446, 297 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612031; Guerlin et al., Nature 448, 889 (2007), arXiv:0707.3880
1.4-20

On resonance an atom turns the reflection from −1 to +1

  • A one-sided cavity: r is the amplitude of the light that comes back
  • On resonance r=−1 when empty, r=(2C1−1)/(2C1+1) with an atom
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 16, on resonance, with no transmission through the back mirror
1.4-21

The π phase shift needs a one-sided cavity with 2C₁ > 1

r(Δ)=1−2κin(γ+iΔ)(κ+iΔ)(γ+iΔ)+g2
  • Δ is the detuning, κin the input mirror's leak rate, κloss every other loss
  • Empty (blue): all the light returns; its phase passes through π on resonance
  • One atom, C1≈3 (orange): the phase is 0 on resonance; 0.49 is scattered
  • The π step needs κin≫κloss (overcoupled), a pulse narrower than κ and a matched beam
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 16; g, κ, γ of Reiserer et al., Nature 508, 237 (2014), arXiv:1404.2453
1.4-22

One reflection changes the sign of one atom-photon state

  • The atom's |⁠↑⁠⟩ couples to the cavity; |⁠↓⁠⟩, a hyperfine splitting lower, does not
  • The photon's polarisation h goes to the cavity, v to a plain mirror: only |⁠h⁠↓⁠⟩ changes sign
Duan and Kimble, Phys. Rev. Lett. 92, 127902 (2004), arXiv:quant-ph/0309187, Fig. 1
1.4-23

Reflections off one atom make a controlled phase flip

  • Two photons in turn: the atom is left free, and only |hh⟩ of the photons changes sign
  • A lost photon, probability Ps≈1/(1+C1), gives no click: a known failure (heralded)
Duan and Kimble, Phys. Rev. Lett. 92, 127902 (2004), arXiv:quant-ph/0309187, Eq. 1 and Fig. 2
1.4-24

One reflection gave the first atom-photon quantum gate

  • One 87Rb atom in a Fabry-Pérot cavity with C1≈3; the photons are weak laser pulses
  • Left: the photon flips if the atom couples, right in 86 %, and stays if not, 99 %
  • Right: from superpositions, atom and photon end in a Bell state, fidelity 80.7(5) %
  • A second photon makes a GHZ state of the atom and two photons: 61(2) %
  • Post-selected on a detected photon; about a third are not reflected
Figure: Reiserer et al., Nature 508, 237 (2014), arXiv:1404.2453, Fig. 1b (left) and Fig. 2 (right)
1.4-25

A photonic-crystal cavity showed the same π phase switch

  • Left: a photonic-crystal cavity, rows of holes in a waveguide that act as mirrors
  • One atom beside it has C1=3.9: the cavity cut its lifetime from 26 ns to 3.0 ns
  • The atom shifts the phase of a weak reflected probe by (1.1±0.1)π (middle)
  • A gate pulse of 0.6 photons on average shifts the atom's phase by (0.98±0.07)π (right)
  • Both post-selected: only runs with an atom in the cavity, and with a reflected gate photon, count
Figure: Tiecke et al., Nature 508, 241 (2014), arXiv:1404.5615, Fig. 1a (left), Fig. 2a (middle) and Fig. 4b (right)
1.4-26

Light outside the cavity mode reflects as off a plain mirror

Rexp=(1−ξ)+ξ|r|2
  • A fraction ξ of the input power is in the cavity mode
  • That part comes back as |r|2; the cavity's reflection coefficient r depends on the atom
  • The rest, 1−ξ, never meets the atom and carries no atom-dependent phase
  • Rexp is the reflected power a detector sees
  • Mode overlap in Reiserer 2014: 92(3) %
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, pp. 9 to 10; mode overlap: Reiserer et al., Nature 508, 237 (2014), arXiv:1404.2453
1.4-27

In a cavity the memory efficiency is set by CN, not by OD

ηmem=(2CN1+2CN)2
  • Atoms in a cavity store a photon as in section 1.2; CN=NC1 replaces the OD
  • On retrieval a share 2CN/(1+2CN), the cavity's β, goes into the mode
  • Storage is retrieval run backwards; the memory efficiency ηmem is their product
  • One atom at C1=25: 98 % per step, 96 % for both; free space needs OD ≈ 300
  • Valid for a leaky cavity, κ≫gN
Cavity: Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033804 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612082; free space: Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033805 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612083
1.4-28

Cavity experiments reach C₁ from 0.22 to 145

  • Each value is C1 with half widths; the paper's own value in brackets
  • The colour is the kind of cavity, pictured at the right
  • The open marker is a preprint's internal value, κloss in place of κ
Figures: Ritter et al., Nature 484, 195 (2012), arXiv:1202.5955, Fig. 1; Grinkemeyer et al., Science 387, 1301 (2025), arXiv:2410.10787, Fig. 1A; Tiecke et al., Nature 508, 241 (2014), arXiv:1404.5615, Fig. 1a; Kato and Aoki, Phys. Rev. Lett. 115, 093603 (2015), arXiv:1505.06774, Fig. 1(a); values from the papers named in the notes
1.4-29

An interface needs large C₁, an overcoupled cavity and mode matching

Pout=κoutκ·2C11+2C1
  • Pout is the share of the atom's emission that leaves through the output mirror
  • Its second factor is β: a large C1 sends the emission into the cavity mode
  • Its first factor, κout/κ, is the share that escapes by the output mirror
  • An overcoupled cavity, κout≫κloss, brings that share near 1
  • Mode matching keeps the incoming light from bypassing the atom
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eqs. 4, 13 and 20; mode matching pp. 9 to 10
1.4-30

Summary of lecture 1

  • One atom takes β≈σ0/2A of a focused beam
  • Tey 2008: 9.8 ± 0.2 % extinction by one atom
  • Many atoms: OD=nσ0L, memory error 5.8/OD
  • A waveguide: β=Γ1D/(Γ1D+Γ′), OD≈2Nβ
  • A cavity: C1=g2/(2κγ), β=2C1/(1+2C1)
  • If 2C1>1, one atom flips the sign of the reflection r
